::: {#exr-miller-int-trig-symmetry}
#### Integral of odd trigonometric functions

Adapted from @problifesavercalc, Question 1.1.34.

Evaluate the integral:

$$\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} (\sin^3 x \cos x + \sin x \cos x)\,dx$$
:::

::: {#sol-miller-int-trig-symmetry}
Because $\sin(-x) = -\sin x$ and $\cos(-x) = \cos x$:

$$\sin^3(-x)\cos(-x) + \sin(-x)\cos(-x) = -\sin^3 x \cos x - \sin x \cos x$$

The integrand is an odd function. The integral of any continuous odd function over a symmetric interval $[-a, a]$ is zero:

$$\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} (\sin^3 x \cos x + \sin x \cos x)\,dx = 0$$

*Alternative (by substitution):* Set $u = \sin x$, so $du = \cos x\,dx$. As $x$ ranges from $-\pi/2$ to $\pi/2$, $u$ ranges from $-1$ to $1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_{-1}^1 (u^3 + u)\,du
&= \sb{\frac{u^4}{4} + \frac{u^2}{2}}_{-1}^1 \\
&= \paren{\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{2}} - \paren{\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{2}} \\
&= 0
\end{aligned}
$$
:::
